narrative:
The model determined that you have a 68.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year grades. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, signaling that your later-year grades raised serious concern about your readiness to pass the bar. Your first-year ranking in the third decile also worked against you, though with less force, reinforcing the same pattern of below-average academic standing.

Your LSAT score of 37 was the only major factor that pulled the prediction in a more positive direction. It sits almost exactly at the average for accepted students, so it helped offset the academic concerns somewhat but was not enough to overcome them.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your law-school grades if you retake courses, consider additional bar-preparation resources, or explore schools with different admissions thresholds that place less weight on early class rank. Reapplying after strengthening the weakest areas would be the most direct next step.
